East Rand Cops

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Beware of being assaulted and extorted on the East Rand - by the cops.

Unique Selling Point:
After years of complaints of brutality and false arrests by Edenvale SAPS, we finally meet the so-called "lawyer" who is the go-to guy for those languishing in police cells. He can get you out and get the Prosecutor to drop the charges - for a fee.
Edenvale Police Station appears to be a free-for-all where police officers have become a law unto themselves. They assault and arrest people on trumped up charges, as a string of J88 medical certificates can prove.

Summary:
Several case studies have come forward since our initial story on gangster cop Goldtooth who assaulted several victims.
This problem seems to be endemic to the East Rand with police members from Edenvale and Sebenza police stations being implicated, as well as members of the EMPD.
Chola Gogwana victim is the daughter of a Colonel in SAPS Crime Intelligence, but when he tried to assist his daughter who was falsely accused of drunk driving, he was laughed at by the constables and told not to interfere. She was then taken to a hospital for a blood test, but while there the SAPS members attacked her, beat and strangled her and filmed the assault on their phone. They then played the video back to her and laughed.

Ilaria di Siena is the mother of a blind child with severe Cerebral Palsy. She was stopped by EMPD and falsely accused of drunk driving. She was arrested and put the back of a police van, her distraught child was then driven to SAPS Edenvale. Her mother was beaten and bruised, and kept overnight in police cells. The next day the charges were dropped.

Further information:
The Dehaloo couple were falsely accused of not stopping at a stop street and taken to the Edenvale police cells. While there a cop brought Mr Dehaloo a cellphone, saying a lawyer wanted to speak to him. The lawyer offered to get them released immediately for R3500 each. He was then taken to his house by 3 SAPS officers so that he was aware that they knew where he lives. He paid the R7000 by e-wallet to Mr" Mangope", and they were released. On the Monday Mngope called Mr Dehaloo demanding another R15000 because he had been to Court on their behalf. He produced a nolle prosequi certificate, signed and stamped by the Prosecutor, T Monareng. The couple refused to pay so much, eventually saying they could maybe pay R3000. They have not heard from Mangope again.
"Mangope"'s name appears to be Winsie Mangombe - there is no lawyer of that name registered with the Law Society or on the Roll of Advocates. His Facebook page reflects posts about clients at various Magistrate's Courts.
Previous web submissions also speak of this so-called lawyer who offers to make charges disappear for a fee.

While in custody, the Dehaloo couple are visited by DA counsellors Simon lapping and Tracey Lourenco. While waiting in the foyer, Trace filmed EMPD officers assaulting a motorist who was asking the SAPS for protection. On seeing her filming, she too was assaulted and her phone confiscated. She, Sher sister, daughter and Simon are now facing charges of assault and resisting arrest.

Script:


EAST RAND COPS

V/O: In 2015 we brought you the story of police brutality in Edenvale. We exposed Constable Mapatlare, the officer with the gold tooth identified by several victims as their assailant. An IPID investigation recommended he be charged with common assault, but the Director of Public Prosecutions declined to prosecute.

Link: It’s been three years since we first exposed police brutality at the Edenvale Police Station, and it seems the only thing that’s changed since then are the station commanders – they’ve had five. Otherwise, it’s business as usual.

V/O: In August a young couple was pulled over by an EMPD officer who arrested them for not stopping at a Stop sign.

Devi: Did you stop at the stop sign?

Nishen: Yip.

Devi: You’re 100% sure?

Nishen: 100% sure.

V/O: The couple asked us to hide their identity for fear of being victimized.

Sandy: They literally demanded a bribe outside Edenvale Police Station. So, I said we’re there, we can go and do it the legal way.

V/O: She called a friend, who alerted local Ward Councillors Simon Lapping and Tracey Lourenco. Accompanied by Tracey’s daughter and sister, they went to the Edenvale Police Station.

Simon: This car came careering into the parking lot and this guy jumped out – young guy – and he went straight off to the Customer Care Centre you could call it – and he requested to open a criminal charge of theft and assault against the EMPD. Shortly thereafter the EMPD came in and there was a woman officer shouting “Arrest this man! Arrest this man!”

Tracey: I thought to myself now I’d better start recording this. They were all pushing him and shoving him, lock him up, and all he wanted to do was open a case. So while the EMPD and the police were crowding around him, I took a step back, still recording. That’s when the Captain saw.

Simon: Tracey was grabbed by at least 3, 4 policemen and was pulled, and I saw them falling down onto the ground, and the policemen were all on top of her, and I just saw boots going in and fists flying.

Devi: Did you get hurt?

Tracey: Yes, I did. I got quite badly hurt. My foot had a torn ligament and a chipped bone, and I had bruises all over my arms, on my legs.

V/O: They were all arrested and detained in the Waiting Cell, while
Tracey’s phone was confiscated.

Tracey: They were doing everything in their power to remove that video.

Simon: Why did they delete the only major piece of evidence that would have exonerated them?

Lungelo: They are not allowed to delete any information from your cellphone or whatever equipment.

V/O: The police are taking Simon and Tracey’s complaints seriously, according to Provincial Spokesperson Colonel Lungelo Dlamini.

Lungelo: If the members of the SAPS are wrong, or maybe there is misconduct on their side, they need to be investigated.

V/O; Ironically the couple they had gone to assist were released before they were, with the help of a lawyer called in by a policeman.

Nishen: Then he told me do you have a lawyer? I said no, I don’t have a lawyer, I was just literally going to the shop. He said wait, I’ll get you a lawyer. Then he phoned, and he gave me the phone. So I spoke to this person on the phone.

Devi: What was the name of the person that you spoke to?

Nishen: Mangope.

V/O: Meet Che Winsie Mangombe Esquire as he refers to himself on Twitter, or Advocate Winsie B Mangombe as he appears on Linked In. This chipper chap is a familiar figure at Edenvale Magistrate’s Court – consulting with clients in the corridors, chatting amicably to Prosecutors with great success. Here he is running up the hill to Edenvale Police Station where he’s a regular visitor. In fact, he’s there so often he doesn’t seem to need an office.

Nishen: Then he said will I be paying for my wife and me, or just for myself? I said no, for the both of us. He thought about it for a while, he said okay I’ll give you a discount, blah, blah, blah.

Devi: Discount? He’s going to give you a discount?

Nishen: Ja, he says it’s going to be R7000 for the both of us to sort everything out. He wanted it to be paid in cash, by eWallet.

V/O: He paid him in three separate payments, and they were released on bail of R500 each. But the following Monday Mangombe wanted more money.

Nishen: It started off at 20 to 30, went down to 15, then other one 8. He really wanted the 8, 8000.

Sandy: So, we negotiated, and we said no 3, because we don’t have that money. Then I said so why don’t you bring it down to 2 because it’s going to be very difficult.

Devi: So, you’re negotiating with him here like you’re in a flea market?

Sandy: Ja.

V/O: According to Mangombe, the additional fee was for getting the charges dropped by the Control Prosecutor. The couple recorded their meeting.

Mangombe: I told them you are not guilty. I gave them my own reasons, you see, on how weak their case is against the two of you.

V/O: When asked for invoices and receipts, he said that meant he would not be able to give them a discount.

Mangombe: If we deviate from the amount that you are actually supposed to charge, it is very unwise for you to actually issue such a receipt.

V/O: But Mangombe is not a member of the Johannesburg Bar, so any tariff guidelines don’t apply. We tried to ask him for an interview.

Devi: Winsie my name is Devi, I’m calling you from a television programme called Carte Blanche on M-Net. I’d like to talk to you about your law practice in Edenvale.

Mangombe: No I’ve got no law practice. I’m an advocate.

Devi: You’re an advocate?

Mangombe: Yes.

V/O: His real name is Bethuel Mangobe. During the time he claims he was a Master’s student at Wits, he was actually an undergraduate at the University of Venda.

Mangombe: Mmm, what’s the problem now?

Devi: There are allegations that you are running a racket with the police.

Mangombe: At which police station now?

Devi: At Edenvale, where you work.

Mangombe: No, I’m not working in Edenvale, I work all over the country.

Devi: So where do you get your clients from, because the allegation is that you get your clients form the policemen who work at Edenvale Police Station?

Mangombe: Ma’am, if there is someone giving me a client, I just go to that person.

Devi: Where did you study?

Mangombe: Ah ma’am, that is not necessary. In fact I don’t like giving out my information to any person.

Devi: Why not, if you’re an admitted advocate?

Mangombe: I don’t even know you, you don’t me.

Devi: I’m telling you who I am, and I’m inviting you to an interview.

Mangombe: No, that invitation is rejected ma’am.

Devi: Oh it’s been rejected, so you give up your right to a reply?

Mangombe: Yes. I don’t care.

Devi: Can I send you questions? Can I send you questions in writing?

Mangombe: No, there’s no such thing. I don’t want to entertain such nonsense from whoever it’s coming from.

Moses: Why would a policeman have a lawyer ready to take on a case of someone arrested by the police? It raises questions.

V/O: IPID is also investigating the complaint against Edenvale police, according to spokesperson Moses Dlamini.

Moses: We are nearing the completion of that investigation.

Link: This is a big intersection in Edenvale where police often pull motorists over. Two months ago they stopped a young student on her way home from her part-time job, but these cops were from Sebenza police station down the road.

V/O: 23-year old Chola Gogwana was with her friend Shantelle when they were pulled over by a female officer who arrested her for drunken driving.

Devi: Had you been drinking?

Chola: Not at all, not at all. She then put her hand through my window, took out my car keys and walked away into the street.

V/O: When Chola followed her, the officer became aggressive.

Chola: She just hit me over the head and was pushing and shoving me back towards my car.

Sfx: Chantal is filming a video. Call my father!
Listen here!
Call my father! Call my father! Call my father! They don’t know that he’s part of the police. Please call my father!

V/O: Colonel Xolani Gogwana is an undercover operative in Police Crime Intelligence and asked us to hide his face. At Sebenza Police Station he introduced himself to the arresting officer, Constable Dlame.

Xolani: I don’t want to interfere I just want to find out what’s going on. She said please, you are wasting our time. They got into the van and drove off.

Devi: You’ve got no idea where Chola has gone?

Xolani: We sat there from 9:30pm until 3:00am the next morning waiting for them to come back.

V/O: For Chola, the nightmare had just begun.

Chola: They took me to a hospital. I’m not sure what hospital it was. They instructed the nurse to give them a minute, to excuse them, they closed the door and continued to beat me up. They were throwing me around, I’m banging on doors, I’m screaming for help and they are laughing, like no-one is going to help you.

Devi: How were they beating you?
04:30
Chola: With closed fists, just hitting me over the head.

Devi; The two of them?

Chola: Shoving me, choking me, now just throwing me around, ja the two of them. The female officer then took out her phone and started recording me. She was like look at you! Look at you!

Devi: Recording you doing what?

Chola: I’m just crying and asking them: guys, why are you touching me? In actual fact, you have no right to do this. She’s like: you have no rights. You have no rights. She was like: you are dirty. Look at you, look at your bra. They have torn my shirt. My ears are ringing even worse now. I can’t see properly from my left eye.

Devi: Did any of the nurses came in to have a look because you were screaming?

Chola: No.

Devi: Did they take your blood then?

Chola: No.

V/O: They then dragged Chola back into the van and drove off to a different police station.

Chola: It was when I got there that some unidentified woman drew blood from my wrist.

Devi: From your wrist?
09:47
Chola: Yes.

V/O: Chola was locked up at Kempton Park Police Station for the night and released on R1000 bail the following afternoon.

Devi: There are so many stories about policemen in this area doing this. What is it about? Why do they do it?

Xolani: We are talking about people that are supposed to defend and protect the citizens of the country. But the citizens of the country are much safer without them being there, than with them being there. Right?

Devi: Do you realize what you are saying?

Xolani: I know exactly what I am saying.

Devi: What were they saying to you while they were hitting you?

Chola: You are spoilt, you need to be taught a lesson. You think because your father is a cop you can do whatever you want. Even if you were the President’s daughter, we don’t care.

Xolani: The biggest issue was she was speaking to her in English. South African police, particularly these junior officers, they are the most xenophobic. They go out there to look for foreigners actually, because they know they are vulnerable. That’s where you get bribes easy.

V/O: The Gogwanas have also laid charges against the police.

Lungelo: I think that police, when they are doing their job they must do their job in a decent manner without resorting to violence.

Moses: It’s totally inappropriate what has happened. Police are not supposed to assault people. The video will be taken as part of the evidence and then we will make recommendations based on what we have picked up during the investigation.

Devi: How has this affected you?

Chola: I t made me feel weak. Even though I was a victim of it, I still sort of feel, felt how could I allow people to violate me like that?

Mangombe: If we deviate from the amount that you are actually supposed to charge, it is very unwise for you to actually issue such a receipt. V/O: But Mangombe is not a member of the Johannesburg Bar, so any tariff guidelines don’t apply. We tried to ask him for an interview. Devi: Winsie my name is Devi, I’m calling you from a television programme called Carte Blanche on M-Net. I’d like to talk to you about your law practice in Edenvale. Mangombe: No I’ve got no law practice. I’m an advocate. Devi: You’re an advocate? Mangombe: Yes. V/O: His real name is Bethuel Mangobe. During the time he claims he was a Master’s student at Wits, he was actually an undergraduate at the University of Venda. Mangombe: Mmm, what’s the problem now? Devi: There are allegations that you are running a racket with the police. Mangombe: At which police station now? Devi: At Edenvale, where you work. Mangombe: No, I’m not working in Edenvale, I work all over the country. Devi: So where do you get your clients from, because the allegation is that you get your clients form the policemen who work at Edenvale Police Station? Mangombe: Ma’am, if there is someone giving me a client, I just go to that person. Devi: Where did you study? Mangombe: Ah ma’am, that is not necessary. In fact I don’t like giving out my information to any person. Devi: Why not, if you’re an admitted advocate? Mangombe: I don’t even know you, you don’t me. Devi: I’m telling you who I am, and I’m inviting you to an interview. Mangombe: No, that invitation is rejected ma’am. Devi: Oh it’s been rejected, so you give up your right to a reply? Mangombe: Yes. I don’t care. Devi: Can I send you questions? Can I send you questions in writing? Mangombe: No, there’s no such thing. I don’t want to entertain such nonsense from whoever it’s coming from. Moses: Why would a policeman have a lawyer ready to take on a case of someone arrested by the police? It raises questions. V/O: IPID is also investigating the complaint against Edenvale police, according to spokesperson Moses Dlamini. Moses: We are nearing the completion of that investigation. Link: This is a big intersection in Edenvale where police often pull motorists over. Two months ago they stopped a young student on her way home from her part-time job, but these cops were from Sebenza police station down the road. V/O: 23-year old Chola Gogwana was with her friend Shantelle when they were pulled over by a female officer who arrested her for drunken driving. Devi: Had you been drinking? Chola: Not at all, not at all. She then put her hand through my window, took out my car keys and walked away into the street. V/O: When Chola followed her, the officer became aggressive. Chola: She just hit me over the head and was pushing and shoving me back towards my car. Sfx: Chantal is filming a video. Call my father! Listen here! Call my father! Call my father! Call my father! They don’t know that he’s part of the police. Please call my father! V/O: Colonel Xolani Gogwana is an undercover operative in Police Crime Intelligence and asked us to hide his face. At Sebenza Police Station he introduced himself to the arresting officer, Constable Dlame. Xolani: I don’t want to interfere I just want to find out what’s going on. She said please, you are wasting our time. They got into the van and drove off. Devi: You’ve got no idea where Chola has gone? Xolani: We sat there from 9:30pm until 3:00am the next morning waiting for them to come back. V/O: For Chola, the nightmare had just begun. Chola: They took me to a hospital. I’m not sure what hospital it was. They instructed the nurse to give them a minute, to excuse them, they closed the door and continued to beat me up. They were throwing me around, I’m banging on doors, I’m screaming for help and they are laughing, like no-one is going to help you. Devi: How were they beating you? 04:30 Chola: With closed fists, just hitting me over the head. Devi; The two of them? Chola: Shoving me, choking me, now just throwing me around, ja the two of them. The female officer then took out her phone and started recording me. She was like look at you! Look at you! Devi: Recording you doing what? Chola: I’m just crying and asking them: guys, why are you touching me? In actual fact, you have no right to do this. She’s like: you have no rights. You have no rights. She was like: you are dirty. Look at you, look at your bra. They have torn my shirt. My ears are ringing even worse now. I can’t see properly from my left eye. Devi: Did any of the nurses came in to have a look because you were screaming? Chola: No. Devi: Did they take your blood then? Chola: No. V/O: They then dragged Chola back into the van and drove off to a different police station. Chola: It was when I got there that some unidentified woman drew blood from my wrist. Devi: From your wrist? 09:47 Chola: Yes. V/O: Chola was locked up at Kempton Park Police Station for the night and released on R1000 bail the following afternoon. Devi: There are so many stories about policemen in this area doing this. What is it about? Why do they do it? Xolani: We are talking about people that are supposed to defend and protect the citizens of the country. But the citizens of the country are much safer without them being there, than with them being there. Right? Devi: Do you realize what you are saying? Xolani: I know exactly what I am saying. Devi: What were they saying to you while they were hitting you? Chola: You are spoilt, you need to be taught a lesson. You think because your father is a cop you can do whatever you want. Even if you were the President’s daughter, we don’t care. Xolani: The biggest issue was she was speaking to her in English. South African police, particularly these junior officers, they are the most xenophobic. They go out there to look for foreigners actually, because they know they are vulnerable. That’s where you get bribes easy. V/O: The Gogwanas have also laid charges against the police. Lungelo: I think that police, when they are doing their job they must do their job in a decent manner without resorting to violence. Moses: It’s totally inappropriate what has happened. Police are not supposed to assault people. The video will be taken as part of the evidence and then we will make recommendations based on what we have picked up during the investigation. Devi: How has this affected you? Chola: I t made me feel weak. Even though I was a victim of it, I still sort of feel, felt how could I allow people to violate me like that? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Beware of being assaulted and extorted on the East Rand - by the cops.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: After years of complaints of brutality and false arrests by Edenvale SAPS, we finally meet the so-called "lawyer" who is the go-to guy for those languishing in police cells. He can get you out and get the Prosecutor to drop the charges - for a fee. Edenvale Police Station appears to be a free-for-all where police officers have become a law unto themselves. They assault and arrest people on trumped up charges, as a string of J88 medical certificates can prove.
metadata.Summary: Several case studies have come forward since our initial story on gangster cop Goldtooth who assaulted several victims. This problem seems to be endemic to the East Rand with police members from Edenvale and Sebenza police stations being implicated, as well as members of the EMPD. Chola Gogwana victim is the daughter of a Colonel in SAPS Crime Intelligence, but when he tried to assist his daughter who was falsely accused of drunk driving, he was laughed at by the constables and told not to interfere. She was then taken to a hospital for a blood test, but while there the SAPS members attacked her, beat and strangled her and filmed the assault on their phone. They then played the video back to her and laughed. Ilaria di Siena is the mother of a blind child with severe Cerebral Palsy. She was stopped by EMPD and falsely accused of drunk driving. She was arrested and put the back of a police van, her distraught child was then driven to SAPS Edenvale. Her mother was beaten and bruised, and kept overnight in police cells. The next day the charges were dropped.
metadata.Further information: The Dehaloo couple were falsely accused of not stopping at a stop street and taken to the Edenvale police cells. While there a cop brought Mr Dehaloo a cellphone, saying a lawyer wanted to speak to him. The lawyer offered to get them released immediately for R3500 each. He was then taken to his house by 3 SAPS officers so that he was aware that they knew where he lives. He paid the R7000 by e-wallet to Mr" Mangope", and they were released. On the Monday Mngope called Mr Dehaloo demanding another R15000 because he had been to Court on their behalf. He produced a nolle prosequi certificate, signed and stamped by the Prosecutor, T Monareng. The couple refused to pay so much, eventually saying they could maybe pay R3000. They have not heard from Mangope again. "Mangope"'s name appears to be Winsie Mangombe - there is no lawyer of that name registered with the Law Society or on the Roll of Advocates. His Facebook page reflects posts about clients at various Magistrate's Courts. Previous web submissions also speak of this so-called lawyer who offers to make charges disappear for a fee. While in custody, the Dehaloo couple are visited by DA counsellors Simon lapping and Tracey Lourenco. While waiting in the foyer, Trace filmed EMPD officers assaulting a motorist who was asking the SAPS for protection. On seeing her filming, she too was assaulted and her phone confiscated. She, Sher sister, daughter and Simon are now facing charges of assault and resisting arrest.
